name: Lipodissolve / PC-DC injections

card.summary: Injected fat-dissolving mixtures (phosphatidylcholine/deoxycholate) that have drawn FDA warnings; the only approved injectable is a separate deoxycholic acid product.
card.aka: Phosphatidylcholine injections, injection lipolysis, PC/DC, mesotherapy for fat
card.note: FDA sent warning letters in 2010 on unapproved lipodissolve products; case reports include infection, scarring and nodules.

quick.overview:
Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis or PC/DC injections, is the practice of injecting a mixture, usually phosphatidylcholine and sodium deoxycholate, into subcutaneous fat to reduce small deposits. In looksmaxxing circles it is mentioned for double chin and facial fat.

Published support consists mostly of retrospective series and practitioner reports; a review noted that no placebo-controlled studies have shown safety or efficacy. A separate, FDA-approved deoxycholic acid product (Kybella) exists for submental fullness.
quick.mechanism: The detergent-like components are described as disrupting fat cell membranes, causing local fat cell breakdown and an inflammatory response that is followed by tissue remodeling. Practitioners also claim skin tightening.
quick.risks: The FDA stated that lipodissolve products are not approved for fat removal and received reports of scarring, skin deformation and painful lumps. Case reports describe infections, including a nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. Professional societies in plastic surgery and dermatologic surgery have issued warnings.

lead: Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis or PC/DC injections, refers to injecting drug mixtures into subcutaneous fat to destroy fat cells. Most formulations are based on phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) [1]. Practitioners have used it for small localized deposits, including under the chin.

Authors of practitioner-written papers report reductions in localized fat and some skin retraction, and describe the method as an alternative or adjunct to liposuction [2][3]. A review noted that no placebo-controlled studies have established safety or efficacy, though many retrospective reports describe benefit [1]. In 2010 the US FDA sent warning letters over lipodissolve marketing [1].
infobox: Not FDA approved for fat removal; FDA warning letters issued April 2010 [1]
Deoxycholic acid (Kybella), approved 2015 for submental fullness [1]

paras: In 1966 researchers found that intravenous phosphatidylcholine solutions could clear fat emboli. A product called Lipostabil, containing 5% PC and 2.5% DC, was approved in Germany for conditions such as fat embolism and dyslipidemia. The first report of using it for fat removal described under-eye fat [1].

Use for body contouring spread in the 2000s, and papers in plastic surgery and dermatology journals described techniques and standards of practice [3][4]. In July 2005 a UK malpractice insurer stopped offering cover for its use, and the UK MHRA warned that the drugs were being unlawfully advertised as fat reducers [1]. On April 7, 2010 the FDA sent warning letters to six US medspas and a Brazilian company, stating these products are not approved for fat removal [1].

A 2005 report by practitioners described fat reduction and skin retraction in small deposits, noting outcomes depend on formula, technique and patient selection [2]. A 2012 paper examined safety, effectiveness and patient satisfaction [6], and a 2009 paper described clinical experience with the technique [7]. A 2011 review described the field as having drawn critical scrutiny from media and the FDA, while newer injectables with detergent activity were in development [4]. The Wikipedia summary notes that no placebo-controlled study has shown safety or efficacy [1].

The FDA received reports of permanent scarring, skin deformation and deep painful knots from unapproved lipodissolve products [1]. A 2022 case report described painful purulent nodules caused by Mycobacterium at injection sites [8], and a 2013 case report described hemorrhagic spots on the abdomen after treatment [10]. Professional bodies including the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, the American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery and the American Society of Dermatologic Surgery have issued warnings [1].

Lipostabil has been approved in Germany for over 40 years, and the technique is widely used in German-speaking countries, where pharmacies compound the formulations [1]. In the US, deoxycholic acid alone (Kybella) was approved in 2015 for moderate to severe submental fullness, a separate regulatory product from PC/DC mixtures [1].

Published human work consists mainly of practitioner series, reviews and case reports [2][3][4][6][7]. Two small trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov: an injection lipolysis study for abdominal fat (n=20, started 2008, completed) [11] and a PC/DC study for localized fat removal (n=18, started 2009, terminated) [12]. No results are given in the available registration records.
